warmup.q: sealed class Extension permits FixedDays, SameAgain {} is not abstract, and FixedDays and SameAgain are its final subclasses. A switch expression over an Extension has case FixedDays f and case SameAgain s and no default. Does it compile?
options: Yes: the permits list is complete, so the switch is exhaustive
No: new Extension() is also a possible value, so the switch misses a case
No: only interfaces can be sealed
Yes, but a plain Extension throws MatchException at run time
warmup.why: A sealed class that isn't abstract can be instantiated itself, so an Extension that is neither FixedDays nor SameAgain can exist, and javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Make Extension abstract, or an interface, and the two cases cover it. Kotlin sidesteps the trap: a sealed class there is always abstract.

opening:
Back at the library desk, the request form has a line near the top: Item type, with four boxes to tick. Book, Disc, Magazine, From another library. Because the form lists every possible answer, the clerk's instruction sheet can have one line per box, and the clerk knows the sheet is complete. Now picture a form where the item type is a blank line instead. Someone writes "board game". The sheet has no line for it, and nobody notices until a board game turns up at the counter.

An ordinary Java interface is that blank line: any class, anywhere, can implement it. So code that handles "each kind of item" can never know it handled them all. The trap is easy to fall into, because the code compiles, the tests pass with today's four kinds, and the fifth kind arrives months later.

Last lesson, a record fixed which boxes one form has. In this lesson, we'll fix which kinds of form exist: seal a type, choose how each branch ends, see where the subtypes may live, and let the compiler find every switch when the list grows. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a form that lists every box to tick, and a blank line that let a board game in. A sealed type is that printed list: javac and the JVM refuse a subtype that isn't on it, and each branch ends final, sealed or non-sealed. In return, every switch without a default is checked against it.

Now look in your own code for an if/else chain of instanceof checks that ends in else throw. That else is a blank line on the form.

Next, we'll meet the clerk who reads these forms. What can a switch do when it can see inside each record, and what does it do with a blank sheet?

sections.h: A sealed type closes the list of direct subtypes
sections.html:
Start with the requests a member can make at the desk: borrow a book, renew a loan, return it. Written as an ordinary interface, Request has three implementations today. Any class in any package can add a fourth, say a Donate next week, and it compiles. Every if/else chain that handles requests skips the newcomer without a word and lands in its final else.

Before JDK 17, the only fix was a trick: an abstract class with a package-private constructor, so that only classes in its own package can extend it. That closes the list, but the compiler still doesn't know what's on it, so it can't check a switch against it.

A sealed type is a class or interface that names its permitted subtypes, the only classes allowed to extend it directly. Add sealed and a permits clause, and the list becomes part of the type:

Java
public sealed interface Request permits Borrow, Renew, Return {}

public record Borrow(String isbn, int days) implements Request {}
public record Renew(int extraDays) implements Request {}
public record Return() implements Request {}
Kotlin
sealed interface Request {
    data class Borrow(val isbn: String, val days: Int) : Request
    data class Renew(val extraDays: Int) : Request
    data object Return : Request
}

In the paperwork picture, a sealed type is a form with a fixed set of boxes to tick. The boxes are printed on the form, so the clerk knows every possible answer.

Sealed classes and interfaces have been a standard feature since JDK 17 (JEP 409, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that added them). javac, the Java compiler, checks the list from both sides. Uncomment Donate in the SealedBasics demo without adding it to the list, and javac stops:

error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Request (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)

javac also writes the list into the class file, as a PermittedSubclasses attribute, a small table the JVM (the program that runs Java code) reads when it loads a class. So the JVM checks it too: a class compiled against an older, unsealed Request fails to load with IncompatibleClassChangeError next to the sealed one. Nobody gets to scribble a fifth box in the margin.

You can leave permits out when every subtype is declared in the same source file. javac then takes the subtypes it finds there. Reflection, the API a program uses to look at its own classes, shows the result: Request.class.isSealed() is true, and getPermittedSubclasses() returns the three records.

Kotlin has no permits clause. Its rule is location: any class in the same package and the same module may extend a sealed type. So class Donate : Request in that package compiles, and the list grows by itself. The same line in another package fails with a class can only extend a sealed class or interface declared in the same package. With the JDK 21 target these labs use, kotlinc 2.4, the Kotlin compiler, writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute as javac. Java code therefore sees a Kotlin sealed interface as sealed: a Java switch over it needs no default, and javac rejects a Java class that tries to implement it.

Sealing restricts direct subtypes only. Renew.class.isSealed() is false. What may sit below each permitted subtype is the next question.

try.title: Break the list on purpose
steps: Run SealedBasics (or SealedBasicsKt) with the command below.
In the Java demo, uncomment static final class Donate implements Request {} and run again. Read the error.
Add Donate to the permits clause and delete final from it. Run again. Then put final back.
Now delete the whole permits ... clause and run. What does getPermittedSubclasses() print?
In the Kotlin twin, uncomment class Donate : Request. Does it compile? Why is that different from Java?

code.title: SealedBasics.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; /** A sealed interface names its direct subtypes, and the JVM keeps that list. */ public class SealedBasics { // the three things a member can ask for at the desk sealed interface Request permits Borrow, Renew, Return {} record Borrow(String isbn, int days) implements Request {} // records are final record Renew(int extraDays) implements Request {} record Return() implements Request {} // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. // static final class Donate implements Request {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Request.isSealed(): " + Request.class.isSealed()); for (Class<?> c : Request.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) { System.out.println("permits: " + c.getSimpleName() + (Modifier.isFinal(c.getModifiers()) ? " (final)" : "")); } System.out.println("Renew.isSealed(): " + Renew.class.isSealed()); } }

alt.title: SealedBasics.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Kotlin has no permits clause: the direct subtypes are the ones declared in this package and module sealed interface Request { data class Borrow(val isbn: String, val days: Int) : Request // final by default data class Renew(val extraDays: Int) : Request data object Return : Request } // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. Then try it in another package. // class Donate : Request /** kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does. */ fun main() { println("Request.isSealed(): ${Request::class.java.isSealed}") for (c in Request::class.java.permittedSubclasses) { println("permits: ${c.simpleName}" + if (Modifier.isFinal(c.modifiers)) " (final)" else "") } println("Renew.isSealed(): ${Request.Renew::class.java.isSealed}") }

try.expect: The first run prints Request.isSealed(): true, the three records marked (final), and Renew.isSealed(): false. The unlisted class fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Request (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). Listed but without a modifier, it fails with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. With no permits clause, javac infers all four from the file and prints Donate (final) too. In Kotlin, class Donate : Request compiles: the list is whatever sits in the same package and module.

video.title: A sealed type prints every box on the form: javac and the JVM refuse an unlisted subtype, and a switch without default finds the new one

sections.h: final, sealed or non-sealed: every branch has to choose
sections.html:
Every permitted subtype of a sealed type must say how its own branch ends, with exactly one of three modifiers. A class that says nothing stops javac with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. An interface can't be final, so for one the message is sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected.

final ends the branch. Records and enums are final already, so a record needs no modifier, which is one reason sealed interfaces and records fit together so well. sealed continues the closed list one level down, with its own permits. non-sealed reopens the branch on purpose: anyone may extend it, in any package.

The library's own list uses all three. Books and magazines are records. Discs are a sealed branch with exactly two kinds, DVDs and audio CDs. And some items are lent to us by partner libraries, which describe them in their own code:

Java
public sealed interface LibraryItem permits Book, Disc, Magazine, PartnerItem {}
public record Book(String isbn, String title) implements LibraryItem {}            // final
public sealed interface Disc extends LibraryItem permits Dvd, AudioCd {}          // closed below
public record Magazine(String title, int issue) implements LibraryItem {}         // final
public non-sealed interface PartnerItem extends LibraryItem {                     // open below
    String partnerId();
}
Kotlin
sealed interface LibraryItem {
    data class Book(val isbn: String, val title: String) : LibraryItem            // final by default
    sealed interface Disc : LibraryItem                                            // closed below
    data class Magazine(val title: String, val issue: Int) : LibraryItem
    interface PartnerItem : LibraryItem { val partnerId: String }                  // open below
}

On the form, non-sealed is the box marked "From another library: ______", with a blank line after it. The clerk can't list every partner's items, but one instruction covers them all: send it back to the library named on the line.

non-sealed sounds as if it defeats the point. It doesn't, because the compiler still knows the shape of the tree. A switch covers the open branch with one case PartnerItem p, and that case matches every partner's class, including ones a partner writes next year. Your switch stays complete, and the partners stay free. Kotlin has no non-sealed keyword: a plain interface, or an open class, under a sealed parent plays the same role.

So "sealed means final" is wrong: a sealed type has subtypes by definition, and a non-sealed branch can have any number. The trap that catches people in code review is a third one. A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value. The NonSealedDemo has a sealed class Extension, the rule for how many days a renewal adds, with two final subclasses, FixedDays and SameAgain. Delete abstract, and new Extension() becomes legal. The switch with one case per subclass then fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, because a plain Extension matches neither case. Make the parent abstract, or make it an interface. Kotlin avoids the trap entirely: its docs say a sealed class is always abstract.

Every branch of a sealed tree ends in final, sealed or non-sealed. Choose each one on purpose.

We know how each branch ends. The next question is where the branches may be written down.

try.title: Reopen one branch, close the trap
steps: Run NonSealedDemo. ArchiveBox is a partner library's code: which modifier lets it exist?
Delete non-sealed from PartnerItem, leaving a plain interface, and run. Read the error, then put it back.
Delete abstract from sealed abstract static class Extension and run again.

code.title: NonSealedDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends as final, sealed or non-sealed. */ public class NonSealedDemo { sealed interface LibraryItem permits Book, Disc, PartnerItem {} record Book(String title) implements LibraryItem {} // final: a leaf sealed interface Disc extends LibraryItem permits Dvd, AudioCd {} // sealed: closed below record Dvd(String title) implements Disc {} record AudioCd(String title) implements Disc {} non-sealed interface PartnerItem extends LibraryItem { // non-sealed: open below String partnerId(); } // a partner library's code: allowed, because PartnerItem is non-sealed record ArchiveBox(String partnerId, String contents) implements PartnerItem {} // Step 3: delete "abstract" here and compile. sealed abstract static class Extension permits FixedDays, SameAgain {} static final class FixedDays extends Extension { final int days; FixedDays(int days) { this.days = days; } } static final class SameAgain extends Extension {} static String describe(LibraryItem item) { return switch (item) { case Book b -> "book " + b.title(); case Disc d -> "disc " + d; // one case for the sealed branch case PartnerItem p -> "partner " + p.partnerId(); // one case for the open branch }; } // how many days a renewal adds to a loan static int extraDays(Extension e, int loanDays) { return switch (e) { case FixedDays f -> f.days; case SameAgain s -> loanDays; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Book("Dune"))); System.out.println(describe(new Dvd("Paddington"))); System.out.println(describe(new ArchiveBox("city-archive", "old maps"))); System.out.println("PartnerItem.isSealed(): " + PartnerItem.class.isSealed()); System.out.println("renewal: " + extraDays(new FixedDays(7), 21) + " and " + extraDays(new SameAgain(), 21) + " extra days"); } }

alt.title: NonSealedDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo // Kotlin subtypes are final unless you open them, and there is no non-sealed keyword: // a plain interface (or an open class) under a sealed parent is the open branch. sealed interface LibraryItem { data class Book(val title: String) : LibraryItem // final: a leaf sealed interface Disc : LibraryItem // sealed: closed below data class Dvd(val title: String) : Disc data class AudioCd(val title: String) : Disc interface PartnerItem : LibraryItem { // open below val partnerId: String } } // a partner library's code, which could live in any package: PartnerItem is an ordinary interface data class ArchiveBox(override val partnerId: String, val contents: String) : LibraryItem.PartnerItem // A Kotlin sealed class is always abstract, so the trap in step 3 of the Java demo can't happen here. sealed class Extension { class FixedDays(val days: Int) : Extension() object SameAgain : Extension() } fun describe(item: LibraryItem): String = when (item) { is LibraryItem.Book -> "book ${item.title}" is LibraryItem.Disc -> "disc $item" // one branch for the sealed branch is LibraryItem.PartnerItem -> "partner ${item.partnerId}" // one branch for the open branch } // how many days a renewal adds to a loan fun extraDays(e: Extension, loanDays: Int): Int = when (e) { is Extension.FixedDays -> e.days Extension.SameAgain -> loanDays } /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends closed, sealed again, or open. */ fun main() { println(describe(LibraryItem.Book("Dune"))) println(describe(LibraryItem.Dvd("Paddington"))) println(describe(ArchiveBox("city-archive", "old maps"))) println("PartnerItem.isSealed(): ${LibraryItem.PartnerItem::class.java.isSealed}") println("renewal: ${extraDays(Extension.FixedDays(7), 21)} and ${extraDays(Extension.SameAgain, 21)} extra days") }

try.expect: The demo prints book Dune, disc Dvd[title=Paddington], partner city-archive, PartnerItem.isSealed(): false and renewal: 7 and 21 extra days. Without a modifier, javac says sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected (an interface can't be final, so final isn't offered). Without abstract, the extraDays switch fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values: a plain Extension is now a possible value. The Kotlin twin can't show that trap, because its sealed class is always abstract.

sections.h: Where the subtypes may live: one package, or one module
sections.html:
Sealing ties a hierarchy to one place, and Java and Kotlin draw the boundary slightly differently.

In Java, the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type. A module here is a named group of packages, described by a module-info.java file. If your code isn't in a named module, the subtypes must be in the same package. Split the sealed interface and its record across two packages, library.api and library.book, and javac refuses:

error: class LibraryItem in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package
public sealed interface LibraryItem permits library.book.Book {}

The wording is clumsy, since it names the sealed interface as the class doing the extending, but the rule is clear. Add a module-info.java that puts both packages in one module, and the same files compile.

Kotlin's rule is the same package and the same module, whether or not you use Java modules. So for most code the two languages agree: keep a sealed hierarchy in one package. That's rarely a burden. The subtypes are usually small records or data classes that read best next to each other, often nested inside the sealed type itself, which also lets Java infer permits.

The rule makes sense once you see what sealing promises. The author of a sealed type says "this is the complete list", and the compiler can only hold everyone to that if the whole list is compiled and shipped together. In the picture, the form and all its boxes come from one print shop. A box printed somewhere else could be reprinted on its own schedule, and every instruction sheet checked against the old form would quietly go stale.

A sealed list must be compiled together. Keep it in one package.

With the list closed and kept in one place, the compiler can finally put it to work.

try.title: Split a hierarchy across packages
steps: The folder labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages holds a sealed LibraryItem in library.api, a Book record in library.book, and a module-info.java. Gradle doesn't compile it; you run javac yourself.
Run the first command. Read the error and the line it points at.
Run the second command, which adds the module descriptor.

Predict, then check: move Book.java into library/api/, change its package line to library.api, change the permits clause to permits Book, and run the first command again (with library/api/Book.java in place of the old path).

code.title: terminal
code.html: cd labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages # 1. class path, unnamed module: two packages are not allowed javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages library/api/LibraryItem.java library/book/Book.java # 2. one named module: two packages are fine javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages module-info.java library/api/LibraryItem.java library/book/Book.java

try.expect: The first command fails with class LibraryItem in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package, pointing at library.book.Book in the permits clause. The second compiles with no output, because both packages belong to the module library. After the move, the first command compiles too: on the class path, one package is enough.

aside.title: Is my program in a module?
aside.html: Probably not. A named module exists only when there's a module-info.java at the root of the source tree. Most applications, including most web services, run from the class path, a plain list of jar files and folders, and everything on it belongs to one unnamed module. So the package rule is the one you'll usually meet. Libraries that ship as modules may split a sealed hierarchy across their own packages.

sections.h: Let the compiler find every switch, and keep default out
sections.html:
Sealing pays off in a switch. Over a sealed type, javac knows every possible subtype, so a switch with one case per subtype is exhaustive: its cases cover every possible value, and it needs no default. javac checks that the cases really do cover every subtype. The StatusSwitches demo has three switches over CopyStatus, where one copy of a book is right now: on the shelf, on loan, on hold for a member, or missing. Here is one of them:

Java
static boolean canLendToday(CopyStatus s) {
    return switch (s) {                              // no default
        case OnShelf shelf -> true;
        case OnLoan loan -> false;
        case OnHold hold -> false;
        case Missing missing -> false;
    };
}
Kotlin
fun canLendToday(s: CopyStatus): Boolean = when (s) {   // no else
    is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> true
    is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> false
    is CopyStatus.OnHold -> false
    is CopyStatus.Missing -> false
}

Now the library starts sending damaged books away to be repaired, and someone adds InRepair to CopyStatus. Every switch over CopyStatus without a default stops compiling. On JDK 21 to 26 the error is the bare one, pointing at the switch:

StatusSwitches.java:30: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
        return switch (s) {
               ^

JDK 27's javac adds the cases you're missing, under a missing patterns: line, here InRepair _. kotlinc has always been specific: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is InRepair' branch or an 'else' branch. Either way, the build hands you a to-do list: every switch that has to learn about repairs.

The third switch isn't on that list. reminderDays ends with default -> 0, which means "and anything else", and the compiler takes it at its word. InRepair drops into the default without a sound and gets 0 reminder days, though the repair has a due date too. A default on your own sealed type throws away the one check sealing gives you. The OpenJDK team's 2026 guide to switching over sealed types has a section called "By default, avoid default", because a default "sweeps errors, both present and future, under the rug".

A default on a list that grows hides the next item. Leave it out.

Keep default for switches where "everything else" really is one answer, such as the illegal (state, event) pairs of a state machine in State and Chain of Responsibility. The same guide asks authors to say in the Javadoc why a type is sealed. Maybe it models a closed set, like the statuses of a copy. Or maybe the author only wants to control who implements it. Say which, and whether you expect to add subtypes, so the people switching over it know what's coming.

Exhaustive has one limit, and it's about time. javac checks a switch against the list it can see when it compiles. A program compiled against the old list can still meet an InRepair from a newer library at run time, and lesson 3 of this track shows what happens then. Sealing also fits only lists you own: a plug-in point that other people extend should stay open.

try.title: Send a copy away for repair
steps: Run StatusSwitches once and look at the three functions: label, canLendToday and reminderDays. Which one has a default?
Add InRepair to the permits clause and uncomment the InRepair record. Before you run, predict which functions javac will report.
Run it, then make it compile again by handling InRepair where javac asked. What does reminderDays return for a copy in repair now? Is that right?
Do the same in the Kotlin twin, StatusSwitchesKt.

code.title: StatusSwitches.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; /** Three switches over one sealed type. Add a subtype and see which ones the compiler finds. */ public class StatusSwitches { // where one copy of a book is right now sealed interface CopyStatus permits OnShelf, OnLoan, OnHold, Missing {} record OnShelf(String shelfmark) implements CopyStatus {} record OnLoan(String memberId, int daysLeft) implements CopyStatus {} record OnHold(String memberId) implements CopyStatus {} record Missing(int daysMissing) implements CopyStatus {} // Step 2: add InRepair to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record InRepair(int daysLeft) implements CopyStatus {} static String label(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { // exhaustive, no default case OnShelf shelf -> "on shelf"; case OnLoan loan -> "on loan"; case OnHold hold -> "on hold"; case Missing missing -> "missing"; }; } static boolean canLendToday(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { // exhaustive, no default case OnShelf shelf -> true; case OnLoan loan -> false; case OnHold hold -> false; case Missing missing -> false; }; } static int reminderDays(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { case OnLoan loan -> loan.daysLeft(); // remind the member before it's due case OnHold hold -> 3; // the member has three days to collect it default -> 0; // "and anything else": the compiler stops checking }; } public static void main(String[] args) { CopyStatus[] copies = { new OnShelf("FIC 12"), new OnLoan("M-1042", 9), new OnHold("M-2210"), new Missing(40) }; for (CopyStatus s : copies) { System.out.printf("%-9s lend today: %-5s reminder in %d days%n", label(s), canLendToday(s), reminderDays(s)); } } }

alt.title: StatusSwitches.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo // where one copy of a book is right now sealed interface CopyStatus { data class OnShelf(val shelfmark: String) : CopyStatus data class OnLoan(val memberId: String, val daysLeft: Int) : CopyStatus data class OnHold(val memberId: String) : CopyStatus data class Missing(val daysMissing: Int) : CopyStatus // Step 2: uncomment this class. Kotlin has no permits clause to edit. // data class InRepair(val daysLeft: Int) : CopyStatus } fun label(s: CopyStatus): String = when (s) { // exhaustive, no else is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> "on shelf" is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> "on loan" is CopyStatus.OnHold -> "on hold" is CopyStatus.Missing -> "missing" } fun canLendToday(s: CopyStatus): Boolean = when (s) { // exhaustive, no else is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> true is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> false is CopyStatus.OnHold -> false is CopyStatus.Missing -> false } fun reminderDays(s: CopyStatus): Int = when (s) { is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> s.daysLeft // remind the member before it's due is CopyStatus.OnHold -> 3 // the member has three days to collect it else -> 0 // "and anything else": the compiler stops checking } /** Three whens over one sealed type. Add a subtype and see which ones the compiler finds. */ fun main() { val copies = listOf(CopyStatus.OnShelf("FIC 12"), CopyStatus.OnLoan("M-1042", 9), CopyStatus.OnHold("M-2210"), CopyStatus.Missing(40)) for (s in copies) { println("%-9s lend today: %-5s reminder in %d days".format(label(s), canLendToday(s), reminderDays(s))) } }

try.expect: The first run prints four lines, from on shelf lend today: true reminder in 0 days to missing lend today: false reminder in 0 days. With InRepair, javac reports two errors, the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, one in label and one in canLendToday. On JDK 27 each also says missing patterns: with InRepair _. reminderDays compiles silently and returns 0 for a copy in repair, which is probably wrong (the repair has a due date too), and nothing told you. kotlinc reports the same two functions with Add the 'is InRepair' branch or an 'else' branch.

compare.title: The copy statuses in Java and Kotlin

java.title: CopyStatus.java
java.html: public sealed interface CopyStatus permits OnShelf, OnLoan, OnHold, Missing {} record OnShelf(String shelfmark) implements CopyStatus {} record OnLoan(String memberId, int daysLeft) implements CopyStatus {} record OnHold(String memberId) implements CopyStatus {} record Missing(int daysMissing) implements CopyStatus {} static String label(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { // no default case OnShelf shelf -> "on shelf"; case OnLoan loan -> "on loan"; case OnHold hold -> "on hold"; case Missing missing -> "missing"; }; }

kotlin.title: CopyStatus.kt
kotlin.html: sealed interface CopyStatus { data class OnShelf(val shelfmark: String) : CopyStatus data class OnLoan(val memberId: String, val daysLeft: Int) : CopyStatus data class OnHold(val memberId: String) : CopyStatus data class Missing(val daysMissing: Int) : CopyStatus } fun label(s: CopyStatus): String = when (s) { // no else is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> "on shelf" is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> "on loan" is CopyStatus.OnHold -> "on hold" is CopyStatus.Missing -> "missing" }

compare.note: The idea is the same and so is the bytecode: both compilers write a PermittedSubclasses attribute, so each language sees the other's sealed types as sealed. Three things differ. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them from one source file) and makes every subtype choose final, sealed or non-sealed; Kotlin's list is whatever is declared in the same package and module, and subtypes are final unless you open them. Java's location rule is the module, or the package on the class path; Kotlin's is always the package and the module. And Kotlin has data object for a case with no fields, where Java uses a record with no components or an enum.

worked.title: Seal the events from the self-service machine

steps.say: The self-service machine by the door sends the library's program an event each time someone uses it. Today there are two kinds, and a handler sorts them with an instanceof chain. Someone adds a third kind to the machine, Renewed. This compiles with no warning, and the handler starts throwing on every renewal.
steps.code: public interface MachineEvent {} void handle(MachineEvent e) { if (e instanceof CheckedOut c) lend(c); else if (e instanceof CheckedIn c) takeBack(c); else throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown event " + e); // Renewed lands here }

alt.html: interface MachineEvent fun handle(e: MachineEvent) { if (e is CheckedOut) lend(e) else if (e is CheckedIn) takeBack(e) else throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown event $e") // Renewed lands here }

steps.say: Seal the event type and make each event a record in the same package. Records are final, so they need no modifier.
steps.code: // 1. close the list public sealed interface MachineEvent permits CheckedOut, CheckedIn, Renewed {} public record CheckedOut(String memberId, String isbn) implements MachineEvent {} public record CheckedIn(String isbn) implements MachineEvent {} public record Renewed(String memberId, String isbn, int extraDays) implements MachineEvent {}

alt.html: // 1. close the list sealed interface MachineEvent { data class CheckedOut(val memberId: String, val isbn: String) : MachineEvent data class CheckedIn(val isbn: String) : MachineEvent data class Renewed(val memberId: String, val isbn: String, val extraDays: Int) : MachineEvent }

steps.say: Replace the chain with a switch that has no default. The chain could never be checked; the switch is checked on every build, and the else throw disappears because there is no "else" left.
steps.code: // 2. one case per event, no default void handle(MachineEvent e) { switch (e) { case CheckedOut c -> lend(c); case CheckedIn c -> takeBack(c); case Renewed r -> extend(r); } }

alt.html: // 2. one branch per event, no else fun handle(e: MachineEvent) = when (e) { is MachineEvent.CheckedOut -> lend(e) is MachineEvent.CheckedIn -> takeBack(e) is MachineEvent.Renewed -> extend(e) }

steps.say: A switch statement with patterns must be exhaustive too, so the void version is checked just like an expression. Last, write down why the type is sealed, so the next person knows that new events will come and that handlers must be updated, not given a default.
steps.code: /** * Every event the self-service machine sends. Sealed because handlers must deal with each one. * New events will be added: expect your switch to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ public sealed interface MachineEvent permits CheckedOut, CheckedIn, Renewed {} // 3. say why

alt.html: /** * Every event the self-service machine sends. Sealed because handlers must deal with each one. * New events will be added: expect your when to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ sealed interface MachineEvent // 3. say why

In LibraryItem, seal the interface, seal Disc, and give PartnerItem the modifier that keeps it open to partner libraries (TODO 1 to 3). Run the tests: four should pass now.

A sealed sub-interface looks like sealed interface Disc extends LibraryItem permits Dvd, AudioCd {}.
sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected means a permitted interface has no modifier; an interface can't be final. Records are final already.

drill.title: Seal a hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a sealed HoldOutcome with three results: Collected(String memberId), Expired(int daysOnShelf) and Waiting, where Waiting is itself sealed, with InTransit (no fields) and OnHoldShelf(int shelf) below it. Then write label(HoldOutcome) with no default, using one case for everything still waiting. Java first, then Kotlin.

answer.html: sealed interface HoldOutcome permits Collected, Expired, Waiting {} record Collected(String memberId) implements HoldOutcome {} record Expired(int daysOnShelf) implements HoldOutcome {} sealed interface Waiting extends HoldOutcome permits InTransit, OnHoldShelf {} record InTransit() implements Waiting {} record OnHoldShelf(int shelf) implements Waiting {} static String label(HoldOutcome o) { return switch (o) { case Collected c -> "collected by " + c.memberId(); case Expired e -> "expired after " + e.daysOnShelf() + " days"; case Waiting w -> "waiting"; // one case covers the sealed branch }; }

alt.html: sealed interface HoldOutcome { data class Collected(val memberId: String) : HoldOutcome data class Expired(val daysOnShelf: Int) : HoldOutcome sealed interface Waiting : HoldOutcome data object InTransit : Waiting data class OnHoldShelf(val shelf: Int) : Waiting } fun label(o: HoldOutcome): String = when (o) { is HoldOutcome.Collected -> "collected by ${o.memberId}" is HoldOutcome.Expired -> "expired after ${o.daysOnShelf} days" is HoldOutcome.Waiting -> "waiting" // one branch covers the sealed branch }

recap: sealed ... permits fixes the list of direct subtypes. javac checks it, and the JVM refuses to load a subclass that isn't on it.
Each permitted subtype is final (records already are), sealed (closed one level down) or non-sealed (open again, and still covered by one case).
A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value, so its subtypes don't cover it. Make it abstract or an interface.
Java subtypes must share the module, or the package on the class path. Kotlin subtypes must share the package and the module.
A switch over a sealed type with no default is checked: add a subtype and every such switch fails to compile. JDK 27 also lists the missing patterns. A default hides the new subtype instead.
The limit: sealing works only for a list you own and compile together. A plug-in point that others extend stays open, and an old program can still meet a subtype it never saw.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown item") to every switch over your sealed LibraryItem, "to be safe". Explain, in your own words, what that costs and when a default is the right call.
explain.answer: Over a sealed type, a switch with no default is checked by the compiler: it knows every subtype, and the build fails if a case is missing. That's the main reason to seal the type. Adding a default tells the compiler "anything else goes here", so when someone adds a new kind of item, every switch still compiles and the new item throws at run time instead, probably at the desk with a member waiting. Without the default, the build gives you the list of switches to update. A default is right only when "everything else" really has one answer, such as rejecting most events in a given state. For a branch others must extend, use a non-sealed subtype and one case for it, not a default.

deeper.html:
Sealing is enforced in three places, and it helps to know which one you're looking at.

javac enforces it at compile time, with the errors in this lesson. The JVM enforces it at load time, from the PermittedSubclasses attribute. Compile final class B implements S against an old, unsealed S, then run it next to a newer S that is sealed and doesn't list B, and class loading fails with java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class B cannot implement sealed interface S. That stops a stray jar from smuggling a subtype into your hierarchy. And reflection reports it: Class.isSealed() and Class.getPermittedSubclasses(), both added with sealed classes, are what the tests in this lesson's lab use.

None of the three stops you from adding a subtype yourself, and that's on purpose. The 2026 Amber guide calls adding a permitted subtype "a permissible and compatible evolution" of a sealed API. Programs compiled against the old list keep loading and running; only their switches change behavior. Recompiled, those switches fail to build. Not recompiled, they meet the new subtype at run time and throw MatchException. The guide describes this as how Java balances "safety with resilience": you find out either at build time or loudly at run time, never silently. Lesson 3 runs that experiment, and shows that the same thing happens for an enum constant added after the switch was compiled.

For Kotlin interop, one detail is worth checking in your own build. The PermittedSubclasses attribute only exists in class files for JDK 17 and later, so Java sees a Kotlin sealed type as sealed only when kotlinc targets 17 or higher. With the JDK 21 target the labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes it, and javac rejects final class Bad implements Status {} against a Kotlin sealed Status with the usual not listed in its 'permits' clause error.
